title: Snap two aluminium framing struts into a square corner on a push-in connector, and prove the joint by lifting the frame
instruction: Join strut B's hollow end onto the corner connector on strut A so that its catch locks and the corner is square, prove the joint by lifting the frame by strut B alone, then set the frame down flat on the table clear of the jig, let go, and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Machine frames, robot cells and test rigs are built from aluminium extrusion joined with push-in corner connectors. The strut being joined has to be held still against the push that snaps the catch, and the joint is checked by lifting the frame by the other strut.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) Strut A: 20 x 20 mm square aluminium tube (6063, 3 mm wall, 14 mm square inside) 26 cm long, 190 g with its connector, lying on the table running away from the arms, from 20 to 46 cm forward, 7 cm left of the centre line. On its near end, a die-cast zinc push-in corner connector: a 20 mm cube on the tube's end with a solid 11 mm square peg 4 cm long pointing to the right, its last 5.5 mm pointed (a 45-degree wedge seen from above). In the peg's top, 15 mm from strut A's side, sits the catch: a red steel spring button 6 mm across and 6 mm long, its tip-side face bevelled at 45 degrees, standing 3 mm proud of the peg; it presses flush against a spring of 1.5 N per mm (4.5 N to press it flush, travel 4.5 mm). (2) Strut B: the same 20 x 20 x 3 mm tube, 24 cm long, 130 g, lying square to A on its right, in line with the peg, its open end (the 14 mm square bore, used as a socket 4.6 cm deep) facing the peg, 1.5 cm short of its tip. An 8 mm wide slot is cut across its top wall from 11 to 19 mm in from its open end, so with B fully on (its end against A's side) the button springs up into it and locks B on. (3) A framing jig: two dark steel strips 3.4 cm long, 4 mm thick and 1.6 cm tall, fixed to the table either side of strut B's end, 1.5 mm clear of it each side. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end. Fully on: strut B's open end within 3 mm of strut A's side with the catch up in B's hole. Square: the two struts' axes 90 degrees apart, within 3 degrees. 1.0: fully on and square, the corner lifted at some point after it snapped on, by strut B alone (strut A's near end at least 2.5 cm off the table with each gripper's fingertip centre (TCP) at least 5 cm from strut A), the frame lying flat on the table again, each TCP at least 5 cm from both struts, and both arms back where they started (each TCP within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: fully on and square; 0.25: strut B at least 1 cm onto the peg; else 0.0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with both struts still.
reset_notes: Press the catch down through the hole and pull strut B off the peg; lay both struts back where they started.
fidelity: Rigid-body PhysX (Isaac Sim 6.1, 20 Hz control) at real size and mass. Simplified: the tubes are plain square bars (the dark lines are drawn only), the peg is a loose 11 mm fit in the 14 mm bore (1.5 mm play each side, a real connector fits closer), and the spring button is a block on a sprung prismatic joint (1.5 N/mm) that B's wall presses down and that rises into B's slot. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
